chapters.title: Unit 3: Properties of Substances and Mixtures

terms.def: A unitless measure of how much light of one wavelength a sample absorbs; 0 means none. Transmittance is the fraction of light that passes through.
The acid dissociation constant, Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA], the equilibrium constant for HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻; pKa = −log Ka, so a smaller pKa means a stronger acid. Kb and pKb do the same for a base.

How fully an acid gives up its proton, measured by Ka. An acid is stronger when its conjugate base is more stable: the negative charge spread by resonance, pulled by electronegative atoms, or held on a large atom.
terms.topicTitle: Molecular Structure of Acids and Bases

terms.def: An acid-base indicator is a weak acid, HIn, whose two forms differ in color; it changes color over about pKa ± 1. Choose one whose pKa is close to the equivalence-point pH.
A solution is acidic when [H₃O⁺] > [OH⁻], basic when [OH⁻] > [H₃O⁺], and neutral when they are equal. Neutral is pH 7.00 only at 25 °C.
The minimum energy a collision must have for the colliding particles to react. It is set by the reaction pathway, not by the temperature.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements that keeps metallic bonding and metallic properties.
Able to act as either an acid or a base, depending on what it reacts with; water and HCO₃⁻ are examples (also called amphiprotic).
A negative ion: it has more electrons than protons, such as Cl⁻.
The inverse of a logarithm: 10ˣ undoes log x and eˣ undoes ln x.
The smallest piece of an element that still has that element's properties.
The mass of an element's atoms in atomic mass units, as listed on the periodic table; numerically the same as the element's molar mass in g/mol.
A unit for the mass of atoms (amu, also called the dalton): one twelfth of the mass of a carbon atom of mass 12, about 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g.
The number of protons in an atom's nucleus, which identifies the element (carbon is 6, oxygen 8).
The size of an atom, measured as half the distance between the nuclei of two touching or joined atoms of the element.
The rule that electrons fill the lowest-energy open subshell first: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, and so on.
The mean mass of an element's atoms, weighting each isotope's mass by its relative abundance; the value on the periodic table.
6.022 × 10²³ per mole, the number of particles in one mole.
A = εbc: absorbance equals the molar absorptivity ε (L/(mol·cm)) times the path length b (cm) times the concentration c (mol/L).
The energy needed to remove an electron from a particular subshell of an atom, a measure of how strongly the nucleus holds it.
The temperature at which a liquid boils. The normal boiling point is at sea-level air pressure; stronger attractions between particles raise it.
The angle between two bonds that meet at the same atom, such as about 104.5° for H–O–H in water.
The energy needed to break one mole of a bond, equal to the depth of the potential energy minimum below zero.
The energy needed to break 1 mol of a given bond in gas-phase molecules, always positive; tables list averages, and ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
The distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, at the minimum of their potential energy curve.
The number of bonding pairs between two atoms (1, 2 or 3); in a resonance hybrid it can be a fraction, such as 4/3 in nitrate.
A pair of electrons shared between two atoms in a covalent bond, drawn as a line in a Lewis diagram.
Breaking or shattering when struck instead of bending; ionic solids are brittle because shifting a layer brings like charges together.
A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a Brønsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor, using a lone pair to bond to the H⁺.

A solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) in similar amounts. Added acid reacts with the base of the pair and added base with the acid, so the pH changes only a little.

How a buffer resists pH change: added H₃O⁺ reacts with the conjugate base and added OH⁻ reacts with the weak acid, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA], and the pH, change only slightly. Dilution leaves the ratio, and so the pH, almost unchanged.

How much strong acid or base a buffer can absorb before its pH changes greatly. It grows with the moles of weak acid and conjugate base, and is greatest in both directions when the two are about equal (pH near pKa).
The flat, slowly rising part of a weak acid or weak base titration curve before the equivalence point, where the weak species and its conjugate are both present.
A long graduated glass tube with a stopcock, used to deliver a measured volume of titrant. It is read at the bottom of the meniscus (the curved liquid surface) to 0.01 mL.
Measuring the energy of a process from the temperature change of a known mass of material, usually water, in an insulated container (a calorimeter); q(process) = −q(water).
A carboxylic acid (–COOH) is a weak acid whose conjugate base, the carboxylate (–COO⁻), is stabilized by resonance. An amine (–NH₂) is a weak base that accepts a proton on its nitrogen lone pair.
terms.topicTitle: Molecular Structure of Acids and Bases

terms.def: A substance that speeds up a reaction by providing a mechanism with lower activation energies. It is used in one step and regenerated in a later one, so it is not consumed overall.
A positive ion: it has fewer electrons than protons, such as Na⁺.
The voltage of an electrochemical cell, E. Under standard conditions E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), where each E° is a standard reduction potential; a positive E°cell means a favored reaction.
The atom in a molecule or ion that is bonded to two or more other atoms; it is drawn in the middle of a Lewis diagram.
An attraction that holds two or more atoms or ions together, caused by nuclei attracting electrons.
A change in which bonds within particles break and new bonds form, producing new substances with new properties.
A statement of a reaction in formulas: reactants, an arrow, then products. Coefficients in front of each formula make the atom counts equal on both sides.
The state of a reversible reaction in a closed system when the forward and reverse rates are equal, so the concentrations of all species stay constant (but are usually not equal).
Element symbols with subscripts that show the ratio of atoms in a substance, such as H₂O (2 H for each O).
A process in which bonds break and form, so the atoms of the starting substances end up in new substances with different properties.
Separating a mixture by how strongly each component is attracted to a stationary phase (paper, a plate or a column) compared with a moving mobile phase. Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent-front distance.
The idea that particles react only when they collide with at least the activation energy and a suitable orientation; such collisions are effective collisions.
P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, for one sample of gas changing conditions; temperatures in kelvin.
Rules for K when an equation is changed: reversing it gives 1/K, multiplying all coefficients by n gives K to the n, and adding equations multiplies their K values.
A reaction of a substance with oxygen gas, usually giving off heat and light. A hydrocarbon (a compound of only carbon and hydrogen) burning in excess oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water.
The lowering of a salt’s solubility in a solution that already contains one of its ions: the common ion raises Q above Ksp, so less salt dissolves. Ksp itself does not change.
A substance made of two or more different elements joined in a fixed ratio, such as water (H₂O) or table salt.
Two species that differ by exactly one H⁺. When an acid gives up a proton it becomes its conjugate base; when a base accepts a proton it becomes its conjugate acid.
In a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
An electron in an inner, filled shell of an atom, closer to the nucleus than the valence electrons.
The force between two charges is proportional to the product of the charges divided by the square of the distance between them (F ∝ q₁q₂/r²): opposite charges attract, like charges repel.
A pair of reactions linked by a shared intermediate, so a thermodynamically favored reaction drives an unfavored one; their ΔG° values add and their K values multiply.
A bond in which two atoms share a pair of electrons that both nuclei attract.
A solid in which every atom is covalently bonded to its neighbors in one continuous web, such as diamond or quartz. Very hard, with very high melting points.
A solid whose particles are arranged in an ordered pattern that repeats in every direction. An amorphous solid, such as glass, has no such long-range order.
Describes electrons that are not held between one pair of atoms but spread over several or many atoms, as in a metal.
Mass divided by volume, usually in g/mL or g/cm³; it can be used to convert between the mass and the volume of a substance.
Making a solution weaker by adding solvent. The moles of solute stay the same, so M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, where V₂ is the final total volume.
Solving a problem by multiplying by conversion factors, ratios equal to 1, so that unwanted units cancel and only the wanted unit is left.
A separation of positive and negative charge, such as the δ+ and δ− ends of a polar bond; drawn as an arrow pointing toward the negative end.
The attraction between the δ+ end of one polar molecule and the δ− end of another.
The attraction between a polar molecule and the dipole it creates in a nearby nonpolar particle.
The separation of an ionic compound into its ions as it dissolves, such as NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
Separating a mixture by boiling off the most volatile component and condensing its vapor. The component with weaker intermolecular forces vaporizes first.
A state in which two opposite processes run at equal rates, so nothing changes overall, such as evaporation and condensation in a sealed container.
The net positive charge a valence electron feels: the nuclear charge reduced by the shielding of the core electrons (roughly protons minus core electrons).
How well a substance carries an electric current; it needs charged particles that can move, such as ions in a melt or solution or electrons in a metal.
A conductor where a half-reaction takes place: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode.
Using an electric current from an outside source to drive a redox reaction that is not thermodynamically favored, as in electroplating or producing a metal from its molten salt.
A solute whose aqueous solution conducts electricity because it contains moving ions. Strong electrolytes give many ions, weak ones few, nonelectrolytes none.
An electrochemical cell in which an outside power supply drives a redox reaction that is not thermodynamically favored.
The full range of electromagnetic radiation, from long-wavelength radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible and ultraviolet light to short-wavelength X-rays.
A tiny negatively charged particle outside the nucleus; it has about 1/1800 of the mass of a proton.
The energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron; atoms that attract an added electron strongly release more energy.
A list of an atom's occupied subshells with the number of electrons in each, such as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ for sodium, or [Ne] 3s¹ in noble gas notation.
A region of electron density around a central atom: one lone pair, or one bond to another atom whether single, double or triple.
A main energy level of electrons in an atom, numbered n = 1, 2, 3…; higher shells are on average farther from the nucleus.
How strongly an atom attracts electrons that it shares with another atom; it rises across a period and falls down a group.
The move of an electron between energy levels, such as from the ground state to an excited state, caused by absorbing a visible or ultraviolet photon of matching energy.
A substance made of only one kind of atom, such as carbon, oxygen or iron.
Measuring how much of an element a sample contains, to identify a compound or to work out how pure a sample is.
A reaction that happens in a single event at the particle level: one collision, or one particle breaking apart. Its rate law follows from its coefficients.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound, such as CH₂O for glucose.
Describes a process that absorbs energy from the surroundings into the system, so the surroundings cool and ΔH is positive.
A graph of a system's enthalpy against the progress of a reaction; the gap between the reactant and product levels is ΔH, and the hump between them gives the activation energy.
A measure of a system's energy; its change, ΔH, is the energy the system absorbs (positive) or releases (negative) as heat at constant pressure.
The energy absorbed to melt 1 mol of a solid at its melting point (ΔHfus; water 6.01 kJ/mol). Freezing releases the same amount.
ΔH for a reaction exactly as written, in kJ per mole of reaction (the amounts given by the coefficients); a thermochemical equation lists it after the balanced equation.

The enthalpy change when a solute dissolves in a solvent, ΔH°soln: the energy absorbed to separate solute and solvent particles minus the energy released as solute-solvent attractions form. With ΔS°soln it gives the free energy of dissolution, ΔG°soln.
The energy absorbed to vaporize 1 mol of a liquid at its boiling point (ΔHvap; water 40.7 kJ/mol). Condensing releases the same amount.
A measure of the number of ways (microstates) the particles of a system and their energy can be arranged; it rises when matter or energy spreads out.

K: the value of products over reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient, for a system at equilibrium at a given temperature. Kc uses molar concentrations, Kp partial pressures; pure solids and liquids are left out.
A particle diagram of a system at equilibrium: its counts of each species stay the same over time. Converted to concentrations, the counts give K.

The point in a titration where the moles of titrant added have reacted exactly, by the mole ratio, with the analyte. The end point is where the indicator changes color, which should be very close to it.
A number known with no uncertainty, such as a count of objects or a defined equality like 1 kg = 1000 g; it never limits significant figures.
Describes a process that releases energy from the system to the surroundings, so the surroundings warm and ΔH is negative.
A species that does not follow the octet rule: an incomplete octet (B in BF₃), an odd-electron species or free radical (NO), or an expanded octet from period 3 on (S in SF₆).
The small raised number that says how many times a base is multiplied by itself; 10³ = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.
Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents, dividing subtracts them, a power of a power multiplies them, 10⁰ = 1, 10⁻ⁿ = 1/10ⁿ, and a square root halves the exponent.
F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻, the charge on one mole of electrons. It links cell potential to free energy, ΔG° = −nFE°.
The amount of substance produced at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed: q = It, moles of electrons = q/F, and the half-reaction converts moles of electrons to moles of product.
Separating an undissolved solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through a filter; the liquid that passes through is the filtrate.
A bookkeeping charge for an atom in a Lewis diagram: valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus half the bonding electrons.
The link between standard free energy change and the equilibrium constant, ΔG° = −RT ln K: a negative ΔG° means K > 1 and a positive ΔG° means K < 1.
An electrochemical cell (also called a voltaic cell) in which a thermodynamically favored redox reaction, split into two half-cells, produces an electric current.
R in PV = nRT: 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) with atm and liters, or 8.314 J/(mol·K) in SI units.
Gibbs free energy, G; its change ΔG = ΔH − TΔS combines enthalpy and entropy into one test of whether a process is favored. ΔG° is the value under standard conditions.
terms.topicTitle: Gibbs Free Energy and Thermodynamic Favorability

terms.def: Finding how much of a substance or ion a sample holds by turning it into a precipitate of known formula, then filtering, drying to constant mass and weighing the solid.
A column of the periodic table (a group or family); its elements have the same number of valence electrons. A row is a period.
The point in a weak acid (or weak base) titration where half the analyte has reacted, at half the equivalence volume. There [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.
The time for a reactant concentration to fall to half its value. For a first-order reaction it is constant: t½ = 0.693/k.
An equation for just the oxidation or just the reduction part of a redox reaction, with the electrons shown, such as Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻.
The energy needed to raise the temperature of a whole object by 1 °C, in J/°C; for one substance, mass × specific heat.

The flow of energy from a warmer object to a cooler one by particle collisions; it continues until both reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium), and energy lost by one equals energy gained by the other.
A graph of temperature against energy added (or time); sloped parts show one phase warming (q = mcΔT), and flat parts show a phase change at constant temperature (q = nΔH).
pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), the Ka expression in log form, for a buffer of a weak acid HA and its conjugate base A⁻. The log is base 10; for a weak base buffer, use pKa of its conjugate acid.
Because enthalpy is a state function (it depends only on the start and end states, not the route), the ΔH of a reaction equals the sum of the ΔH values of any steps that add up to it.
An equilibrium with species in more than one phase, such as a solid and a gas; pure solids and liquids are left out of its K. A homogeneous equilibrium has every species in one phase.
A mixture whose composition differs from place to place, such as sand in water.
A mixture with the same composition all the way through, such as salt water or air.
The mixing of a central atom's valence orbitals to match its electron domains: sp for 2 domains, sp² for 3, sp³ for 4.
The surrounding of a dissolved particle by water molecules. Around a cation, water's oxygen points in; around an anion, a hydrogen points in.
A strong dipole-dipole attraction between an H atom bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of another molecule.
The ion H₃O⁺, a water molecule bonded to an extra proton. Acids in water give hydronium ions; H⁺(aq) is shorthand for it.
A table with rows for Initial, Change and Equilibrium concentrations of each species. The change row is x times each coefficient, so one known value gives all the others.
PV = nRT: the equation linking the pressure, volume, kelvin temperature and moles of a gas that behaves ideally.
A substance added in small amounts to the analyte that changes color when the first slight excess of titrant is present, marking the end point of a titration.
An equation linking a reactant concentration to time, such as ln[A]t − ln[A]0 = −kt for a first-order reaction.
An attraction between separate particles (molecules, atoms or ions), as opposed to a bond inside one particle. Intermolecular forces are much weaker than covalent bonds.
An alloy in which much smaller atoms fill the gaps between the host metal's atoms, making it harder and less malleable (steel: carbon in iron).
A force between the atoms inside one particle: covalent, ionic or metallic bonding.
An atom or group of atoms with an electric charge, because it has gained or lost electrons.
The attraction between an ion and the oppositely charged end of a polar molecule, such as Na⁺ and the oxygen end of water.
The Coulombic attraction between oppositely charged ions, usually formed when a metal gives electrons to a nonmetal.
A compound made of cations and anions held together by their opposite charges, in the ratio that makes it neutral; its simplest unit (such as one NaCl) is a formula unit.
The size of an ion. A cation is smaller than its atom, and an anion is larger than its atom.
A solid made of a repeating three-dimensional array (a crystal lattice) of cations and anions, each ion surrounded by ions of opposite charge.
The energy needed to remove an electron from an atom or ion in the gas phase; the first ionization energy removes the most loosely held electron.
Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons, and so different masses.
For an acid and its conjugate base, Ka × Kb = Kw (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C), so pKa + pKb = 14.00. The weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base.
The SI unit of temperature. Its zero is absolute zero, the coldest possible temperature; K = °C + 273.15.
The situation in which a thermodynamically favored process (ΔG° < 0) is too slow to observe because its activation energy is very large; the reactants are kinetically stable.
The energy of motion, KE = ½mv². The average kinetic energy of gas particles is proportional to the kelvin temperature.

The kinetic molecular theory: a model of an ideal gas as tiny particles in constant random motion that do not attract each other and collide elastically, with average kinetic energy proportional to kelvin temperature.
The ion product of water, Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻]. It equals 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C and rises with temperature, because water's self-ionization, 2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻, absorbs heat.
The energy needed to separate one mole of an ionic solid into ions far apart; larger ion charges and smaller distances make it larger.
The law that a given compound always contains the same elements in the same proportions by mass, however it is made.
When a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, volume or temperature, it shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change.
A drawing of a molecule or ion that shows every valence electron, with bonding pairs as lines and lone pairs as pairs of dots.
The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first and so sets how much product can form; any reactant left over is in excess (the excess reactant).
The graph of concentration data that comes out as a straight line for a given order: [A] vs t (zero), ln[A] vs t (first) or 1/[A] vs t (second). Its slope gives k.
The exponent that 10 must be raised to in order to give a number: log 1000 = 3 because 10³ = 1000. Also called the base-10 or common logarithm.
The attraction between momentary dipoles in neighboring particles. It acts between all particles and grows with polarizability and contact area.
A pair of valence electrons on one atom that is not shared in a bond; also called a nonbonding pair.
The scale of things you can see, touch and measure in bulk, such as color, mass or volume, as opposed to the particle level.
The ability of a solid to be hammered or bent into a new shape without breaking (ductile: drawn into wire); metals have it because their layers slide while the electron sea holds them.
The number of protons plus neutrons in an atom's nucleus, written as in carbon-14 or ¹⁴C.
The share of a compound's mass that comes from one element: the element's mass in one formula divided by the molar mass, times 100.
A graph from a mass spectrometer showing the masses of the ions in a sample and how many of each there are; for an element, one peak per isotope.
The mass of an ion divided by its charge (m/z), the quantity a mass spectrometer sorts by; for a 1+ ion it equals the mass.
A graph of the fraction of gas particles at each speed (or energy). A higher temperature or a lighter gas moves its peak to higher speeds and flattens it.
The doubt in the last digit of every measurement, set by how finely the instrument can be read.
The temperature at which a solid turns to liquid. Stronger attractions between particles raise it.

An element, on the left or in the middle of the periodic table, that holds its few valence electrons loosely and tends to lose them; nonmetals (upper right) tend to gain electrons, and metalloids lie between.
The attraction between metal cations and the sea of delocalized valence electrons around them.
A solid held together by metallic bonding: metal cations in a sea of delocalized valence electrons.
Finding the orders of a rate law by comparing the initial rates of trials in which only one starting concentration changes.
A prefix that scales a unit by a factor of ten, such as kilo (1000), centi (1/100), milli (1/1000), micro (one millionth) and nano (one billionth).
Two or more substances together but not bonded into one kind of particle, in proportions that can vary.
The mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole (g/mol); the sum of the atomic masses of every atom in one particle.
The number of moles of a salt that dissolve per liter of saturated solution (mol/L), often written s.
Concentration in moles of solute per liter of solution (mol/L, written M).
The counting unit of chemistry: 6.022 × 10²³ particles of whatever you name (atoms, molecules, ions).
The moles of one component divided by the total moles of a mixture. In a gas mixture, P(A) = X(A) × P(total).
The actual number of each kind of atom in one molecule, a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, such as C₆H₁₂O₆.
The arrangement of the atoms (not the lone pairs) around a central atom, such as linear, bent, trigonal planar, trigonal pyramidal or tetrahedral.
Whether a molecule has a net dipole: it is polar when its bond dipoles do not cancel because of its shape.
A solid made of separate molecules held to each other by intermolecular forces. Molecular solids are soft, melt at low temperatures and do not conduct electricity.
Energy held in a molecule's bond vibrations or rotation. Infrared light changes vibrational energy; microwaves change rotational energy.
The number of reactant particles that come together in an elementary step: unimolecular (one), bimolecular (two) or termolecular (three, rare).
Two or more atoms held together as one particle, such as a water molecule, H₂O, or an oxygen molecule, O₂.
The energy profile of a reaction with several elementary steps: one peak (transition state) per step, with intermediates in the valleys between peaks.
A logarithm with base e (about 2.718), written ln. ln x is about 2.303 times log x.
E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q: the cell potential under nonstandard conditions. For a galvanic cell (E° > 0), E > E° when Q < 1, E < E° when Q > 1, and E = 0 at equilibrium (Q = K).

An equation for a reaction in solution that shows only the species that change. The molecular equation writes whole formulas; the complete ionic equation splits every dissolved ionic compound into ions; removing the spectator ions gives the net ionic equation.

The overall change in a reversible reaction when the forward and reverse reactions run at different rates: a net forward reaction turns reactants into products overall, a net reverse reaction the opposite.
A reaction between an acid and a base; for hydroxide bases the net change is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
A particle with no charge in the nucleus of an atom, with almost the same mass as a proton.
An electron configuration with the same arrangement as a noble gas, such as Na⁺ and F⁻ (both like neon). Particles with the same number of electrons are isoelectronic.
The small, dense center of an atom, made of protons and neutrons, which holds almost all of the atom's mass.
The pattern that atoms of period 2 in stable molecules end up with eight valence electrons around them (hydrogen with two).
A region around the nucleus where an electron is likely to be found; each holds at most two electrons. An s subshell has 1 orbital, p has 3 and d has 5.
A factor of ten. Two quantities that differ by a factor of about 1000 differ by three orders of magnitude.

A bookkeeping charge given to each atom as if every bond were ionic, with shared electrons assigned to the more electronegative atom (also called oxidation state). A rise means electrons were lost; a fall means electrons were gained.
The oxidizing agent takes electrons from another species, so it is itself reduced; the reducing agent gives electrons to another species, so it is itself oxidized.
An acid in which the acidic H is bonded to an O that is bonded to a central atom (H–O–X), such as HOCl or HNO₃. More O atoms or a more electronegative central atom makes it stronger.
terms.topicTitle: Molecular Structure of Acids and Bases

terms.def: A charge smaller than one full electron charge, written δ+ or δ−, on the atoms of a polar bond.
The pressure one gas in a mixture would exert alone in the same container. The partial pressures add up to the total pressure (Dalton's law).
A drawing of a substance at the level of its particles (atoms, molecules, ions), with a key to the symbols.
The share of a weak acid that has ionized at equilibrium: [H₃O⁺]eq / [HA]initial × 100%. It rises as the acid is diluted.
The chart of all the elements in order, with each element's symbol and atomic mass, arranged so that elements with similar properties fall in the same column.
A property that changes in a regular way across a period or down a group of the periodic table, such as atomic radius or ionization energy.
pH = −log[H₃O⁺], a base-10 logarithm scale of hydronium concentration; pOH = −log[OH⁻]. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.00. One pH unit is a factor of ten in [H₃O⁺].

A slightly soluble salt whose anion is a base (the conjugate base of a weak acid, such as F⁻, CO₃²⁻ or OH⁻) dissolves more as pH falls: H₃O⁺ removes the anion, Q drops below Ksp, and more solid dissolves. Salts of anions from strong acids (Cl⁻, NO₃⁻) are not affected.
A change of state (melting, freezing, vaporization, condensation, sublimation, deposition) that rearranges particles but does not change what they are.
A method that uses high-energy light to eject electrons from atoms and measures the energy needed to remove each one, giving one peak per subshell.
A single packet of light energy. Higher-energy photons can knock electrons out of atoms.
The energy of one photon, E = hν = hc/λ, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant. Energy levels are quantized, so only photons of matching energy are absorbed or emitted.
A change in the arrangement, spacing or state of particles that leaves the particles themselves unchanged, so no new substance forms; melting, boiling and dissolving are examples.
A covalent bond in which the shared electrons are pulled closer to the more electronegative atom; if the atoms are identical the sharing is equal and the bond is nonpolar.
How easily a particle's electron cloud is distorted. More electrons, held farther from the nucleus, make a particle more polarizable.
A charged group of atoms held together by covalent bonds, such as NH₄⁺ or SO₄²⁻.
An acid that can give up more than one proton, one at a time (diprotic H₂A, triprotic H₃A). Each proton has its own Ka, and a titration curve can show one equivalence point per proton.
Stored energy due to position. For two opposite charges it is lower (more negative) the larger the charges and the closer they are, so separating them takes energy.
A graph of the potential energy of two atoms against the distance between their nuclei; its minimum gives the bond length and the bond energy.
The approximation that a fast reversible step before the slow step has equal forward and reverse rates, used to express an intermediate's concentration in terms of reactants.
An insoluble solid that forms when solutions are mixed; precipitation is the forming of that solid.

A precipitation reaction forms an insoluble solid when two solutions are mixed. Reactions are also described by their pattern: synthesis (substances combine into one), decomposition (one substance breaks into several), single replacement (an element replaces another in a compound) and double replacement (two compounds swap partners).
How closely repeated measurements agree with each other. Accuracy, a different idea, is how close they are to the true value.
The force per unit area from gas particles hitting a surface. 1 atm = 760 torr = 760 mm Hg = 101.325 kPa.
Product-favored: a reaction with K much greater than 1, whose equilibrium mixture is mostly products. Reactant-favored: K much less than 1, mostly reactants with a little product.
A positively charged particle in the nucleus of an atom; the number of protons decides which element an atom is.
Which form of an acid is in the majority: the protonated form (HA) when pH < pKa, the deprotonated form (A⁻) when pH > pKa, equal amounts when pH = pKa. Each pH unit away from pKa is a tenfold ratio.
Matter with a fixed composition throughout: an element or a single compound.
The share of a sample, by mass, that is the substance you want: mass of that substance ÷ mass of the sample × 100.

Justifying a shift by comparing the reaction quotient with the equilibrium constant: Q < K means net forward reaction, Q > K net reverse, until Q = K. Concentration and volume changes move Q; temperature changes move K.
terms.topicTitle: Reaction Quotient and Le Châtelier's Principle

terms.def: The constant k in a rate law. It is fixed for a reaction at a given temperature, rises with temperature, and has units that depend on the overall order.
An equation, found by experiment, that gives the rate of a reaction in terms of reactant concentrations: rate = k[A]^m[B]^n.
The slowest elementary step in a mechanism. It limits the overall rate, so the overall rate law follows from it.
A starting substance in a chemical reaction, written on the left of the arrow; the new substances formed, on the right, are the products.
A graph of the potential energy of reacting particles against reaction progress (the reaction coordinate), from reactants through the transition state to products.
A species made in one step of a mechanism and used up in a later step. It does not appear in the overall equation.
The series of elementary steps by which a reaction happens. The steps must add up to the overall balanced equation.
The exponent on a concentration in a rate law (0, 1 or 2 in this course). The overall order is the sum of the exponents.
A drawing of the particles before and after a reaction. It conserves every atom, and the change in particle counts shows the ratio given by the coefficients.
Q: the same expression as K, filled in with the concentrations or pressures present at any moment. Q < K means net forward reaction, Q > K net reverse, Q = K equilibrium.

How fast the concentration of a reactant or product changes with time, usually in M/s. The average rate is measured between two times, the instantaneous rate at one moment, and the initial rate at the start.
A gas whose particles have volume and attract each other, so it departs from PV = nRT. Deviations are largest at high pressure and low temperature and for particles with strong attractions.

A reaction in which electrons move from one species to another. Oxidation is loss of electrons (oxidation number rises); reduction is gain of electrons (oxidation number falls). The two always happen together.
The share of an element's atoms that are one particular isotope, usually given as a percent.
The description of a species by two or more Lewis diagrams that differ only in where electrons are placed; the real species is a single hybrid of them.
A reaction or step that runs in both directions, written with ⇌. The forward reaction turns reactants into products; the reverse reaction turns products back into reactants.
A tube or porous barrier of an inert electrolyte that lets ions move between the half-cells, keeping each electrically neutral and completing the circuit.
A way to write a number as a coefficient of at least 1 and less than 10 multiplied by a power of ten, such as 6.50 × 10⁻⁷.
The way inner electrons partly cancel the nucleus's pull on outer electrons by repelling them, so outer electrons feel less attraction.
A sigma (σ) bond has its shared electrons along the line between the nuclei (every single bond, and the first bond of a multiple bond); each extra bond in a double or triple bond is a pi (π) bond.
The digits in a measurement that carry meaning: every certain digit plus the one estimated digit. Leading zeros are not significant.
The number of electron pairs shared between two atoms: one in a single bond, two in a double bond, three in a triple bond.

A shortcut for ICE-table problems with a small K: x is dropped where it is added to or subtracted from a starting concentration, then checked; the change should be under about 5% of the starting value.

The amount of a substance that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. Substances dissolve well when solute-solvent attractions are comparable to the solute-solute and solvent-solvent attractions they replace ("like dissolves like").
Ksp: the equilibrium constant for a slightly soluble salt dissolving, equal to the product of its ion concentrations in a saturated solution, each raised to its coefficient. The solid is left out.
A homogeneous mixture: a solute (the dissolved substance) spread evenly through a solvent. In an aqueous solution, the solvent is water.
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C; for liquid water, 4.18 J/(g·°C). It appears in q = mcΔT.
An ion that is dissolved and unchanged on both sides of a reaction in solution, so it is left out of the net ionic equation.

An instrument that passes light of a chosen wavelength through a sample in a cuvette and measures its absorbance. Measurements are made at λmax, and a calibration curve of standards gives an unknown's concentration.
c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s, the speed of all electromagnetic radiation in a vacuum; c = λν links wavelength and frequency.
ΔH°f: the enthalpy change for making 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states (their most stable forms at 1 atm, usually 25 °C); it is zero for an element in its standard state.
The entropy of one mole of a substance in its standard state, S°, in J/(mol·K); it is positive for every pure substance above 0 K. ΔS° of a reaction is Σ nS°(products) − Σ nS°(reactants).
Solid, liquid or gas: the arrangement and motion of a substance's particles. Solid particles vibrate in place, liquid particles slide past each other, gas particles fly freely far apart.
A label after a formula that says how the species exists: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.
Using the mole ratios given by the coefficients of a balanced equation to find the amounts of reactants and products; a mole ratio such as 2 mol H₂O / 1 mol O₂ is the conversion factor.
Standard temperature and pressure: 0 °C (273.15 K) and 1 atm. One mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at STP.

An acid that ionizes fully in water, so [H₃O⁺] equals the acid concentration: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, HClO₄ and the first proton of H₂SO₄. A strong base dissociates fully into OH⁻: the group 1 hydroxides and Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂ and Ba(OH)₂.
terms.topicTitle: pH and pOH of Strong Acids and Bases

terms.def: A part of an electron shell with its own energy, labeled s, p or d, holding at most 2, 6 or 10 electrons.
An alloy in which atoms of similar size take the places of some host metal atoms (brass: zinc in copper).
The system is the part of the universe being studied, usually the reacting particles; the surroundings are everything else, such as the water, container and air.
The theoretical yield is the most product the limiting reactant can make; the actual yield is the amount collected; percent yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100.
The energy a sample holds because its particles move. Heating a sample adds thermal energy.
A process is thermodynamically favored when ΔG < 0: it can proceed on its own, without a continuous input of energy, though possibly very slowly.
terms.topicTitle: Gibbs Free Energy and Thermodynamic Favorability

terms.def: A method for finding the amount of a substance (the analyte) by adding a solution of known concentration (the titrant) from a buret until the two have reacted in the mole ratio of the balanced equation.
A graph of pH against volume of titrant added. Its steep rise (or fall) is centered on the equivalence point; its shape shows whether the acid or base is strong or weak.
The highest-energy arrangement of atoms along a reaction path, with bonds partly broken and partly formed. It cannot be isolated.
The agreed-on amount that a measurement counts in, such as the gram, the liter or the second; a number without its unit is incomplete.
An electron in the outermost occupied shell of an atom; valence electrons take part in chemical reactions.
The pressure of a substance's vapor in equilibrium with its liquid (or solid) in a closed container. It rises with temperature and is higher for liquids with weaker intermolecular forces.
A flask made to hold one exact volume, marked by a line on its neck; used with an analytical balance to prepare solutions of known molarity.
Valence shell electron pair repulsion: the model that electron domains around a central atom repel and spread as far apart as possible, which sets the molecule's shape.
The distance between neighboring crests of a wave (λ). Frequency (ν) is the number of crests passing a point per second; shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy per photon.
An acid that ionizes only partly in water (Ka much less than 1), so at equilibrium most of it stays as whole HA molecules. A weak base, such as NH₃, accepts protons from water only partly.
